items.title: CSD-HOU-25-005, Plan to End Chronic Homelessness Mid-Year Update
notes:
Peter Sweeney, Commissioner of Community Services, introduced the report and Chris McEvoy, Manager of Homelessness and Supportive Housing, and Jennifer Gordon, Manager of Homelessness and Supportive Housing, to provide a presentation on the Plan to End Chronic Homelessness (PECH) Mid-Year Update. A copy of the presentation is attached to the original agenda. J. Gordon provided background for PECH reminding the Committee of the endorsement of the PECH on April 9, 2023. She described PECH as a government-community collaborative, multi-year plan aimed at achieving functional zero chronic homelessness in the region through systems change work. She highlighted various achievements from the $10.2 million 2024 budget, ongoing equity work within PECH, and the impact of the point-in-time count.

J. Gordon further highlighted the concept of functional zero, clarifying that it does not mean no one will ever experience chronic homelessness, but that it commits to making such experiences rare, brief, and non-recurring, with no more than three individuals experiencing chronic homelessness at any given time. The PECH is strategically focused on preventing inflow into homelessness, supporting people to quickly exit homelessness, and preventing repeated episodes. She also introduced the PECH co-creators, a group of over 125 individuals from 65 organizations and community groups, including those with lived experience, working collaboratively on this initiative. Subgroups focused on systems change priorities and a coordinating team were expected to launch soon.

C. McEvoy presented the results of the point-in-time count conducted on October 22, 2024, with the involvement of over 40 community partners. He explained that the PIT count measures sheltered, unsheltered, and hidden homelessness, providing a local and national snapshot. He expressed gratitude to participating organizations and co-creators. Key findings from the 2024 count included an estimated 2,371 individuals experiencing homelessness, with 1,790 completing a voluntary survey, of whom 78% reported experiencing chronic homelessness. The count also showed an increase in emergency shelter and transitional housing use, attributed to service expansions. He emphasized that this data, while concerning, aligns with trends across the province and country, underscoring the need for equity-centered, systems-level solutions informed by lived experience and highlighting housing as a critical social determinant of health. He noted that this data would inform their strategic plans and actions.

C. McEvoy outlined the current priority areas within PECH, which include increasing equitable access through dedicated rental supplements for Black, racialized, and Indigenous individuals; reducing inflow through eviction prevention and rent banks; increasing outflow through investments in supportive housing; and developing a data strategy to monitor outcomes. He provided a snapshot of early outputs, highlighting that investing in housing is more cost-effective than managing emergency shelter use. He noted that 54% of PECH investments directly contribute to limiting inflow and increasing outflow.

J. Gordon concluded by emphasizing that the PECH is focused on building equity into the support system, driven by feedback from co-creators, Council, and lived experts. She provided examples of growing system responsiveness, such as rebuilding services for women, trans, two-spirit, and gender-diverse individuals, including 67 intentional shelter spots and a new transitional housing project for racialized women and children. Additionally, 151 rent subsidies were co-created and set up with 27 organizations, aiming for geographic equity and specifically supporting equity-owed individuals. Staff will be providing an update on the PECH later this year.

Responding to the Committee, P. Sweeney explained the crucial role of rent supports in reducing chronic homelessness globally. He acknowledged situations where partnerships with landlords require addressing repairs and mentioned that the region provides capital grants and loans to landlords and uses insurance and sometimes regional funds to cover repair costs, stressing the importance of maintaining positive relationships with private landlords in a limited supply market. He thanked the landlords and co-creators for their vital contributions.

In response to the Committee, P. Sweeney acknowledged the concerns expressed by the Committee and the community in regards to the recently approved by-law related to the 100 Victoria Street encampment. He stated that staff are meeting with co-creators individually and that they will continue to focus on the goal of ending chronic homelessness, acknowledging that the path to that goal can sometimes be challenging.

C. McEvoy explained that the developing data strategy would include a monthly dashboard tracking inflow and outflow, aiming to reduce the active number to zero. He noted that, while the number of chronic homelessness experiences continues to increase, the rate of growth has slowed compared to the previous year. He pointed to investments in rental supplements with supports and in therapeutic and affordable supportive housing as contributing to moving people out of homelessness and strategically targeting episodic homelessness with rental supplements to prevent chronic homelessness. C. McEvoy further explained that the functional zero target of three individuals experiencing homelessness is a national standard established by the Canadian Alliance to End Homelessness and he believes its an achievable standard. Staff clarified the definition of experiencing homelessness and the challenges of enumerating hidden homelessness, noting ongoing efforts to improve this.

D. Craig requested information on the cost of shelter beds and hospital beds and an update on the YWCA in Cambridge. Staff acknowledged the need for services to support youth and outlined programs like host homes and youth outreach and that a co-developed rural strategy is also being prioritized. P. Wolf noted that the negative stereotypes associated with those needing affordable housing and homelessness and that the associated stigma should be combatted through data-informed decisions and recognizing individual humanity.

In response to the Committee, staff highlighted ongoing collaborations with healthcare partners such as hospitals and Ontario Health Teams.

The Committee expressed the importance of illustrating the achievements gained from the significant investment into the PECH and its overall impact on the Community.

Received for information.

items.title: CSD-HOU-25-006, Racialized Women Transitional Housing Program
notes:
Ryan Pettipiere, Director of Housing Services, introduced the report CSD-HOU-25-006 Racialized Women Transitional Housing Program. He highlighted the program is a partnership with the Coalition of Muslim Women to provide inclusive transitional housing support for racialized women, aligning with the plan to end chronic homelessness and addressing gaps in support for equity-owed groups. The program will offer wraparound staff supports, focusing on social connections, financial stability, and securing permanent housing.

Responding to the Committee, R. Pettipiere confirmed that staff have existing disaggregated data from the point-in-time count and will collect more as the program operates. He explained that the Region is providing the funding and the Coalition of Muslim Women provides support services. He further confirmed that the support provided is non-religious and that the funding for this program is being funded through the current operational budget.

Received for information.

items.title: Strategic Priority - Equitable Services and Opportunities
CSD-CHS-25-001, Canada-Wide Early Learning and Child Care (CWELCC) Directed Growth and Child Care Funding Update
notes:
Barb Cardow, Director of Children`s Services, provided an update on the Canada-Wide Early Learning and Child Care Directed Growth and Child Care Funding. She highlighted that there will be an increase in allocated child care spaces to 4,136 by the end of 2026, along with $1.66 million in additional startup grant funding and $6.3 million from a new infrastructure fund for non-profit spaces. Despite this growth, the waitlist for child care has grown significantly to 13,000 children, with 8,700 needing immediate care. She noted that there was the change in the non-profit to for-profit space allocation, now at 90% non-profit and 10% for-profit for new spaces created since 2024. The 10% for-profit allocation is currently maxed out.

The Committee expressed concern related to insufficient childcare spaces, provincial funding, and the provincially mandated ratio of 90% non-profit and 10% for-profit spaces. Staff are advocating that this ratio be updated to a 70/30 non-profit to for-profit.

In response to the Committee, B. Cardow confirmed that Staff are looking at all options, including regional lands, modular child care, and encouraged the cities and townships to consider using their spaces.

The Committee expressed support for continued advocacy for more funding to reduce the waitlist for childcare spaces.
